Musk said the decision was taken in order to make room for increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi. The move comes after years of weaker-than-expected sales for the futuristic electric pickup.

Tesla will begin winding down production of its Cybertruck around the middle of 2027, as the company shifts its focus towards autonomous vehicles, CEO Elon Musk announced on his social media platform X on Friday.

The decision marks a major shift for Tesla's electric pickup programme, which has struggled to meet the sales expectations set by the world's richest man.

Musk did not clarify whether production would be moved to another facility or whether the vehicle would be discontinued altogether. He also did not address what would happen to outstanding orders.

Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill described the pickup as an "incredible technology development platform" that would live on through the Cybercab.

Musk later reassured owners that the existing Cybertruck fleet would remain on the roads for a long time, calling the production wind-down "the end of an era".

Sales fall short of Musk's ambitions

Unveiled in November 2019, the Cybertruck was presented as a radical departure from traditional pickup trucks, with its angular design and stainless-steel exterior.

Musk initially said the vehicle had attracted around 250,000 pre-orders within days of its unveiling, while Tesla built its Texas production facilities with ambitious plans to manufacture hundreds of thousands of units annually.

However, production was repeatedly delayed, with the first customer deliveries only beginning in late 2023.

The vehicle has struggled to achieve the mass-market appeal Musk had anticipated. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates cited by the Associated Press, US Cybertruck sales fell by 48% in 2025 compared with the previous year, to 20,237 vehicles.

Tesla does not publish separate sales figures for the Cybertruck. Its third-quarter 2026 delivery report showed 8,295 vehicles delivered in its 'Other Models' category, which also includes the Semi and remaining Model S and Model X vehicles.

The pickup has also faced several recalls and quality-control issues, while its unconventional design has divided consumers.

The Cybertruck never made it to Europe

Despite its high-profile launch, the Cybertruck never entered the European market.

Its heavy construction and angular design have raised questions over compliance with European vehicle safety requirements, particularly rules designed to protect pedestrians and other vulnerable road users.

The truck's sharp-edged stainless-steel body and weight have also fuelled debate over whether such vehicles are compatible with European road-safety standards.

The model has therefore remained largely a North American phenomenon, limiting its potential international customer base.

Its public image has also become increasingly tied to Musk's political activities. The Tesla chief's close association with US President Donald Trump and his role in the administration's Department of Government Efficiency made the vehicle a political symbol for some supporters and critics alike.

Some owners have reported vandalism and harassment, further complicating the pickup's public perception.

Tesla bets on driverless future

The decision to free up factory space for the Cybercab reflects Musk's broader ambition to transform Tesla from an electric-car manufacturer into a company focused on artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous transport.

Unveiled in 2024, the two-seater Cybercab is designed to operate without a steering wheel or pedals and is central to Tesla's plans for a driverless taxi network.

The company has already begun offering limited robotaxi rides in the United States, although the technology remains under regulatory scrutiny.

Tesla has said it intends to make the Cybercab a central vehicle in its future transport network, with Musk arguing that autonomous driving and robotics will become increasingly important to the company's business.

The Cybertruck's production wind-down marks a significant change of direction for a vehicle once presented as one of Tesla's most ambitious projects. Whether it disappears from the company's product line altogether, however, remains unclear.

“The European market is the best market in the world,” says investment expert Jan Růžička, urging policymakers to accelerate EU accession and the Capital Markets Union to maintain momentum and sustain enthusiasm among candidate countries.

It’s been over 13 years since a country last joined the European Union. Now, there are nine official candidate countries, some of which, such as Albania, expect negotiations to conclude as early as 2027.

But what does EU enlargement actually mean for the economy and investment opportunities? Does having more members mean more complexities? Does an influx of cheap labour spell disaster for incumbent members? And who stands to gain the most?

In this episode of The Big Question, Angela Barnes is joined by Jan Růžička, Chief External Affairs Officer at PPF Group, a privately held investment group founded in the Czech Republic, to discuss the biggest opportunities and risks of EU enlargement.

What are the biggest commercial opportunities presented by EU enlargement?

When predicting the biggest opportunities arising from this latest wave of accession, Jan looked to past successes. The largest enlargement took place in 2004, when 10 new countries, including his own, the Czech Republic, joined the EU.

Countries with cheap labour, a skilled workforce and traditional industries, such as Poland and the Czech Republic, have boomed over the past two decades. Jan therefore believes that countries like Moldova and Ukraine, which share similar attributes, have good prospects following accession.

“Five-six years ago, people said, ‘Do we need defence? Do we need heavy machinery? Do we need steel factories? Now again, it's very important.”

“In the case of Ukraine, of course, the defence tech, this is something that we don't have so much now in Europe. So I now see, for example, Ukrainians not only asking for investments, but I see Ukrainian investors coming to Europe,” Jan added.

He also stressed the importance of joining the single market, which would allow SMEs to access support.

“Sixty-five percent of our economy, including EU 15, EU 27, candidate countries, are small businesses. They are driving our economies and they are the reason for which we, bigger companies, are successful.”

“EU enlargement will let grow the businesses of small and medium-size companies which then will drive valuation of ourselves as well,” Jan continued.

Are enlargement candidate countries appealing to investors?

PPF Group, the independent, family-owned investment group for which Jan works, already has investments in businesses in the candidate countries of Serbia, Moldova and Ukraine.

“We as PPF, we vote with our money. We are divesting from Asia and investing much more here,” Jan explained.

“Not only because this is a great single market, but rule of law, democracy, predictability, all of this is positive. The European market is the best market in the world.”

Despite Jan’s enthusiasm for EU enlargement and the benefits it could bring to both candidate countries and incumbent members, he acknowledged that the process is not without risks.

He particularly criticised the slow pace at which the Commission is conducting negotiations, arguing that this is discouraging investment.

“I think that the biggest risk is to lose the momentum. [...] Let's not forget that you don't need 27 members to agree. You need 28 as we learned in Iceland, so we need to have some popularity of the EU in those countries and we are losing it,” Jan explained.

(In case you’re not familiar, Iceland was granted candidate status in 2010, with negotiations suspended in 2013. In August 2026, a referendum saw voters reject the resumption of its EU accession process. You can read more about that here.)

To prevent a loss of momentum and enthusiasm during negotiations, Jan suggested granting candidate countries certain limited access rights.

“Maybe it's only the single market, maybe it’s some freight agreement plus, but this is better than to wait for full enlargement.”

Comisia Europeană a constatat, vineri, în mod preliminar, că TikTok încalcă Regulamentul privind serviciile digitale (DSA) din cauza așa-numitului efect de “gaură de iepure” (algoritmi care conduc utilizatorii într-un cerc repetitiv de recomandări – n.r.) prezent pe platforma sa. “Este pentru prima dată când abordăm cu adevărat în mod direct modelul sistemului de recomandări bazat pe interacțiuni cu platforma”, a declarat un oficial al Comisiei, sub protecția anonimatului, pentru Politico. 

Comisia a constatat că TikTok nu a evaluat în mod adecvat riscul ca algoritmul său să îi atragă pe utilizatori în “spirale de conținut”. Algoritmul ține cont de videoclipurile pe care utilizatorii le urmăresc sau le apreciază pentru a le recomanda conținut similar. De exemplu, dacă o persoană urmărește frecvent videoclipuri despre slăbit sau despre aspectul fizic, TikTok poate interpreta acest lucru ca fiind un semn de interes și va arăta tot mai multe videoclipuri pe aceleași subiecte. Astfel, utilizatorul vede în mod repetat același tip de conținut, care poate avea efecte negative asupra bunăstării sale, “inclusiv sentimente crescute de tristețe sau anxietate, nemulțumire corporală, stimă de sine mai scăzută sau agravarea tulburărilor de alimentație și a condițiilor mentale existente”, precizează Comisia. 

“Cu cât un utilizator interacționează mai mult cu un anumit tip de conținut, cu atât algoritmul de alimentare «Pentru tine» (recomandări personalizate – n.r.) al TikTok recomandă mai mult conținut similar. Acest design poate fi dăunător atunci când o astfel de expunere nesfârșită și repetată implică, de exemplu, conținut despre tristețe, izolare sau imagine corporală. Aceste «găuri de iepuri» pot avea un impact negativ asupra sănătății mintale a utilizatorilor, în special a adulților și a minorilor vulnerabili”, arată Comisia Europeană. 

Constatările prezentate azi de către Comisie arată, de asemenea, că TikTok nu a reușit să pună în aplicare măsuri de atenuare proporționale, rezonabile și eficiente pentru a aborda aceste riscuri. Deși platforma încearcă să le recomande utilizatorilor videoclipuri din categorii diferite, aceștia primesc în continuare și frecvent conținut similar, inclusiv conținutul legat de problemele de sănătate mintală și de nemulțumire față de propriul corp.

În plus, opțiunile precum “Nu mă interesează”, care pot fi selectate când interacționezi cu conținutul de pe platformă, nu reușesc întotdeauna să schimbe recomandările. Astfel, algoritmul acordă mai multă importanță timpului petrecut vizionând videoclipurile decât preferințele exprimate de utilizatori. 

Prin urmare, Comisia consideră că TikTok trebuie să modifice secțiunea “Pentru tine” , astfel încât utilizatorii să aibă mai mult control asupra conținutului recomandat, iar algoritmul să nu mai favorizeze timpul de vizionare. Mai mult, recomandă creșterea accesibilității și testarea regulată a algoritmilor. 

În cazul în care opiniile Comisiei sunt confirmate în cele din urmă, ByteDance, care deține TikTok, riscă o amendă de până la 6% din cifra de afaceri anuală globală, dacă nu reușește să rezolve această problemă.

Un purtător de cuvânt al TikTok a respins acuzațiile și a afirmat că compania “are un istoric solid” în ceea ce privește protejarea utilizatorilor săi. “Comisia a făcut o serie de declarații care sunt fundamental inexacte și denaturează arhitectura platformei noastre și angajamentul nostru față de siguranța utilizatorilor”, a declarat purtătorul de cuvânt. Acum, compania poate să analizeze probele, să-și apere practicile și să încerce să elaboreze un plan de remediere a problemelor care să fie acceptabil pentru autoritatea de reglementare, pentru a evita amenzile.

Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said some of the children appeared to be as young as 10 or 11.

Iran’s Security Council chief, Mohsen Rezaei, went to Moscow to deliver a personal message from Ayatollah Khamenei and discuss building a pipeline to import Russian gas.

Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, where he delivered a personal message from Iran’s Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei regarding the Iran war and discussed what both sides called “strengthening ties”.

Iran’s top security official described the meeting as an "extremely important exchange of views," which covered "the post-war situation and regional security.”

Russia has been a long-standing supporter of Iran, purportedly supplying Tehran with intelligence and equipment during the war. Tehran has previously backed Russia in its all-out invasion of Ukraine, and provided its Shahed drone technology.

Moscow has since cloned it into its domestically-made Geran UAVs, which it commonly uses in its daily strikes on infrastructure and civilian targets in Ukraine.

The meeting, which was not announced in advance, follows the Russian president's meeting with his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow during a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum last week.

The content of Khamenei’s message to Putin was not made public, Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported.

"The construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran was discussed" during the meeting with Putin, Rezaei stated.

He explained that the project aims to help Tehran "address its gas shortages, while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighbouring countries."

Although Iran is a major producer of natural gas, it has long suffered from shortages of the fuel, a crisis that has only intensified since the onset of the Iran war in late February.

According to Tehran, during the most intense phase of the war — which lasted nearly 40 days — the US and Israel launched strikes against critical Iranian infrastructure, including gas processing plants.

Iran responded by attacking what it said were US military facilities and other interests in the broader Middle East region. Regional governments, witnesses on the ground and Euronews journalists reported the strikes also hit civilian and infrastructure targets.

Both sides also imposed concurrent blockades of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the world's gas and oil trade.

In early October, Putin stated that Russia is prepared to act as a mediator to help end the war. Moscow has not acted as an intermediary in the talks. Pakistan and Qatar have so far served as the main mediators.

Rezaei noted that Putin emphasised the need for regional security mechanisms and asserted that "any interference by external powers" in resolving the situation in the Middle East is unacceptable.

Russia has delayed, deflected to Kyiv or otherwise rejected all attempts to broker an end to its ongoing war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year.

Infrastructure and Loans

According to Rezaei, the meeting also addressed progress on key bilateral infrastructure projects. "The Supreme National Security Council has approved the executive agreement for the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway, with Russian participation," he said, as cited by the Iranian news agency IRNA.

"The Minister of Roads and Urban Development will soon sign this contract on behalf of the Islamic Republic of Iran," Rezaei added.

Spanning just over 160 kilometres, this section represents the final missing link in the western route of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), which is intended to provide a direct connection between Russia and Iranian ports on the Persian Gulf.

Press reports citing the semi-official Iranian news agency Fars indicated that Russia had finalised preparations to provide Iran with a $1 billion loan, though the transfer of funds has been delayed.

According to Fars, this $1 billion is intended to be the first instalment of a planned $20 billion Russian loan to Iran.

Some experts have linked the delay in disbursing these funds specifically to the stalled progress of the Rasht–Astara railway project.

"We are prepared to provide the necessary credit resources," Putin stated during a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club on 1 October.

"The question is for our Iranian friends to complete their part of the work at this stage."

After the meeting, the Russian Foreign Ministry issued a warning travel advisory telling Russians to avoid visiting Iran and the Middle East while the risk of renewed war persists.

The Russian Foreign Ministry had previously advised Russian citizens against travelling to Persian Gulf countries for tourism — specifically in February, right before the US and Israel launched their attacks on Iran in the opening salvo of the war.

That advisory was lifted in June after Washington and Iran signed an interim deal, which has since collapsed.

Uzbekistan says it harvested more than five million tonnes of raw cotton in 2026, its largest crop since gaining independence in 1991. Officials put the increase at around a quarter from last year. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has set a higher yield target for 2027.

Agriculture Minister Ibrokhim Abdurakhmonov told journalists that the 2025 harvest stood at around four million tonnes. This year's crop also exceeded the government's initial target of 4.5 million tonnes.

Uzbekistan attributes the increase to new cotton varieties, revised planting methods and wider use of harvesting machines. The government says the area planted with cotton has fallen by 38% in recent years and average yields have risen from 2.1 to 5.6 tonnes per hectare.

More than 3,000 machines picked around 85% of the crop in 30 to 35 days, according to the government. It said machines picked the entire crop in Jizzakh and Syrdarya.

From raw cotton to finished textiles

The higher output comes as Uzbekistan expands domestic processing, aiming to turn more of its cotton into yarn, fabrics and clothing at home.

"We used to sell only cotton fibre," Abdurakhmonov told journalists, describing the shift towards manufacturing.

"How do we create added value? New brands, new clothing, new domestic production. We are seeing good businesses emerge," he said.

Much of this activity takes place through cotton-textile clusters linking farms, processors and manufacturers.

According to the World Bank, Uzbekistan has had enough capacity to process its entire raw cotton crop into yarn since 2023. That represents a shift away from dependence on exports of unprocessed fibre.

The Bank estimates that the textile industry employed around 600,000 people in 2024, up from 188,000 in 2018. Many of those workers are women and young people.

Labour reforms

Uzbekistan has also changed how it harvests cotton. For decades, teachers, students and public-sector employees were mobilised for compulsory work in the fields.

From 2017, Uzbekistan introduced reforms aimed at ending forced labour and changing how cotton was produced.

In March 2022, the International Labour Organization said systemic forced and child labour had been eliminated during the 2021 harvest. Its monitoring found that 99% of cotton pickers interviewed had worked voluntarily.

That same month, the Cotton Campaign lifted its call for a global boycott of Uzbek cotton, which 331 international brands and retailers had backed.

The government expects cotton farmers to earn a combined net profit of 13–14 trillion Uzbek soums (about €1bn) from this year's harvest, although the final figures have yet to be confirmed.

Addressing the water challenge

Water use remains a major challenge for cotton farming in Uzbekistan's dry climate. Agriculture accounts for about 90% of the country's water consumption, according to the World Bank.

President Mirziyoyev said cotton farming used half as much water as it did in the 1990s, attributing the reduction to water-saving technologies.

Abdurakhmonov said farmers were switching from flooding fields to drip irrigation, estimating that the technology could reduce water use by around 40%.

"Previously, we flooded the fields, and the soil could not breathe. Microbial activity had declined. Now the soil is recovering," he said, adding that farmers were also rotating cotton with wheat to improve soil conditions.

The government says it is also changing how it grows cotton in areas with salty soils and seeking to reduce fertiliser use.

The target for 2027

Following the record harvest, Mirziyoyev has set a target of raising the national average cotton yield from 5.6 to between 6.5 and seven tonnes per hectare in 2027.

The planned measures include higher-yielding varieties, agricultural drones, artificial intelligence and more efficient irrigation systems. How those measures will affect farmers' incomes and water use remains to be seen.

The European Commission has identified four Mediterranean countries as facing migratory pressure, opening the door to asylum seeker relocations. The Ceuta crisis will have little impact on numbers, while Hungary and Slovakia have failed to contribute to EU solidarity efforts.

Spain, Italy, Greece and Cyprus are considered “under migratory pressure” by the European Commission, according to a report presented on Friday that sets the framework for relocating asylum seekers across the EU in 2027.

The assessment marks the start of the process of redistributing asylum seekers across the bloc, which is likely to prove controversial after EU governments recently clashed over migration, with some countries reluctant to participate.

The Commission said it had taken account of the arrival of more than 80,000 irregular migrants in Ceuta at the end of July, although the report formally covers the period from July 2025 to June 2026.

In just two days, more migrants entered the Spanish exclave than were recorded crossing all EU borders irregularly in the first six months of 2026.

However, the mass arrival is not expected to lead to a proportionate increase in the number of asylum seekers relocated next year.

“There was a strong reaction [to the crisis], and within a very short period the vast majority of those who entered voluntarily returned to Morocco,” an EU official said.

How the solidarity system works

Next year, the four countries under pressure will benefit from the solidarity of other member states, which can take the form of relocating asylum seekers to their territory or of financial contributions.

The report also identifies 15 states “at risk of migratory pressure”: Belgium, Czechia, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, France, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovenia and Finland. They must show solidarity with the countries under pressure, but their situation will be reassessed to avoid disproportionate obligations the following year.

A third group is classed as “facing a significant migratory situation”: Bulgaria, Czechia, Estonia, Croatia, Austria and Poland. They can request an exemption from their solidarity quotas, which the Commission must certify and the other member states approve.

Alongside the report, the Commission proposed an “Annual Solidarity Pool”, which sets the total number of asylum seekers to be relocated across Europe and each country’s share, whether in relocations or in payments to offset them.

The pool’s size has not been made public. Under the law, it must be at least 30,000 relocations and €600 million in financial contributions.

Every member state except those under migratory pressure must contribute in proportion to its population and GDP. Countries can choose between three options: relocating asylum seekers to their own territory, paying €20,000 for each person they do not relocate, or funding operational support in countries under pressure.

EU governments will decide the final size of the pool and each country’s share by the end of the year.

In 2026, national governments significantly watered down the Commission’s proposal. Fewer than 9,000 asylum seekers were effectively relocated, against an agreed reference figure of 21,000.

Hungary and Slovakia fail to meet solidarity obligations

The Annual Asylum and Migration Report also assessed member states’ solidarity to date, flagging problems with Hungary and Slovakia.

The Commission acknowledged that both countries have breached the rules by failing to pledge any relocations or financial contributions for 2026, but no infringement procedures will be launched for now.

“The system is mandatory. Last year, they did not pledge. We are in contact with both member states to see how we can get respect of this dimension,” an EU official said.

Budapest and Bratislava remain opposed to the solidarity system set out in the Pact on Migration and Asylum, as migration is a deeply divisive issue among their citizens.

Italy also came under scrutiny after several member states called on Rome in late August to take back asylum seekers who had entered the EU through its borders before moving to other countries.

Under EU rules, the Commission can suspend solidarity towards a country under migratory pressure if it fails to meet its obligations.

“This is not the case for the time being,” an EU official said.

During the reporting period, around 13,000 transfers back were carried out between member states, although the Commission did not provide country-specific data. Eurodac data also suggest that unauthorised movements within the EU fell by around 13%.

Scientists used AI to design a vaccine capable of protecting against a wide range of bird flu variants. That’s a game changer for national biosecurity and more resilient public health systems, they say.

Scientists at Cambridge University have developed a new vaccine using Artificial Intelligence that targets multiple strains of bird flu in one shot, rather than providing immunity to one variant. The jab could protect even from variants that haven’t emerged yet, they say.

The vaccine is part of a new generation of vaccines targeting multiple strains of the same virus, with the aim of better preparing for future health emergencies, including those involving currently unknown threats.

“Rather than providing immunity to a single variant of bird flu, our new broad-spectrum vaccine is protective against a huge range of variants,” said Jonathan Heeney, from the Lab of Viral Zoonotics at the University of Cambridge, who led the work.

“It’s designed to anticipate viral evolution, rather than reacting to it,” he added.

The study, published in Cell Reports Medicine, found that the new vaccine provides broader protection and superior survival rates compared to standard candidate vaccines that target only one strain currently stockpiled for pandemic preparedness.

Like the coronaviruses that caused COVID-19 and many other emerging infectious diseases, bird flu is an RNA virus. RNA viruses represent a particular threat to human health because they can mutate rapidly into new strains that can jump from animals to humans and evade our immune systems — and the protection offered by existing vaccines.

Current pandemic preparedness relies on stockpiling vaccines against individual virus variants that have already emerged. These new-generation vaccines are a game changer for national biosecurity and more resilient public health systems, the authors noted.

“We can be prepared to respond immediately to virus epidemics and pandemics, rather than the current scenario of always being on the back foot and responding with a strain which will have changed,” said Heeney.

New-generation vaccines

The researchers collected genetic sequence data from bird flu viruses recorded by surveillance programmes worldwide, including samples from wildlife, livestock and humans infected with bird flu.

They used computational and evolutionary algorithms to design five AI-optimised synthetic antigens representing the global diversity of bird flu viruses and helping prevent the virus from evading immune protection.

The active ingredient in a vaccine, called an antigen, triggers the body’s immune system to produce a protective response. This trains the body to fight off future infections caused by a pathogen containing this specific antigen.

“Using AI vastly speeds up the process of vaccine design, and then we can test the vaccine candidates in the lab to make sure they’re robust and safe,” said Heeney.

In the new study, the vaccine completely protected mice and ferrets against a range of genetically distinct variants of the virus that causes bird flu — all of which have caused human infections and represent potential pandemic threats. Only half the animals survived exposure to these same viruses when immunised with the World Health Organization's existing bird flu vaccine.

The next step is to test the new bird flu vaccine in human clinical trials, to make it available for use in the event of an outbreak and to expand the new framework to seasonal influenza vaccines and other rapidly evolving RNA viruses

Developed by the University of Cambridge and its company DIOSynVax Ltd, this is the latest in a series of new vaccines whose active ingredient is designed to give lasting protection from thousands of virus variants in a single vaccine.

Earlier this year, the team developed the first fully AI-designed vaccine to be tested in humans, offering lasting protection against a broad range of viruses — such as Ebola and members of the coronavirus group — even as they mutate.

Co-chaired by Azerbaijani Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov and Ukrainian First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Denys Shmyhal, the delegations signed a formal Protocol and adopted a comprehensive Action Plan for 2026-2027.

The strategic agreements cover 14 distinct sectors, with a strong focus on energy infrastructure resilience and cross-border commercial ties amid severe wartime logistical hurdles.

Grid defence and emergency energy assistance

A critical focus of the Uzhhorod summit was the physical protection and stabilisation of Ukraine's national energy grid ahead of the winter months.

First Deputy Prime Minister Shmyhal and Shahbazov toured a western Ukrainian energy facility to inspect "second-level protection" systems designed specifically to defend critical power infrastructure against ongoing Russian military attacks.

During the site visit, officials confirmed the delivery of the latest Azerbaijani emergency equipment shipment, valued at $1.47 million (€1.32 million).

This strategic dispatch includes nine industrial transformers, 186 kilometres of high-voltage cables, generators, and 12 kV electrical distribution gear required for rapid grid repairs.

"We express our gratitude to Azerbaijan for its constant and substantial assistance in recovery efforts following Russian strikes," Shmyhal stated on X following the inspection.

"We are particularly grateful for transformers, generators, and everything else energy workers need."

Official data released during the commission session indicates that bilateral trade turnover increased by 10.5% over the first eight months of 2026, driven directly by a 17% rise in Azerbaijani exports to Ukraine.

Total mutual investments between the two nations reached $513.5 million (€460 million).

To anchor these commercial ties, both governments are actively pivoting toward industrial localisation and technological partnerships to rebuild Ukraine's heavy industrial base.

"Ukraine is interested in joint production, localisation in Ukraine, and technological partnerships," Shmyhal noted on X, extending a direct invitation to Azerbaijani firms to invest in distributed energy projects and logistics.

In response, the Azerbaijani delegation pitched the Alat Free Economic Zone as a primary tax-free logistics hub for joint enterprise-level collaboration.

The summit officially concluded with a targeted site visit to the Khust Industrial Park, where officials inspected a wind turbine manufacturing facility and the Azerbaijani-owned ATEF enterprise to assess direct opportunities for joint production.

Brussels says TikTok's recommendation algorithm risks exposing children and vulnerable users to harmful content. The platform has rejected the findings as "fundamentally inaccurate".

Europe warned TikTok on Friday that it must change the "harmful" design of its personalised 'For You' feed or risk large fines under the bloc's digital rules, after finding preliminary evidence of violations.

The European Commission accused the social media platform of breaching the Digital Services Act (DSA) over the "harmful 'rabbit holes' effect", where TikTok's algorithm repeatedly recommends similar videos, potentially exposing children and vulnerable users to increasingly harmful content.

"The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's 'For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content," the European Commission said in a statement.

"This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image," it added.

TikTok rejected the Commission's findings, saying they misrepresent how its platform works and the measures it has taken to protect users.

"The Commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform's architecture and our commitment to user safety. We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience," a TikTok spokesperson told Euronews Next.

TikTok's algorithm continues to recommend similar videos even when users indicate they are not interested in certain content.

The European Commission said TikTok had taken steps to address these risks, but they had not been effective enough, calling for further changes to the platform's design.

Among its recommendations, Brussels urged TikTok to give more weight to users' preferences, warning that the "not interested" button "may not be enough to change the content feed".

The Commission also suggested that TikTok stop using viewing time to recommend videos, make user controls easier to access and use, and regularly test its algorithm.

EU steps up efforts to enforce the DSA

The EU has stepped up efforts to protect children online through the DSA, a wide-ranging rulebook that requires tech companies to follow a legal framework. Companies failing to do so face hefty financial penalties and investigation into their platforms.

The Commission launched its investigation into TikTok over possible breaches of the DSA more than two years ago.

Earlier this year, it issued two other sets of preliminary findings, accusing the platform of using "addictive design" features that encourage compulsive use among children and failing to adequately protect children's privacy rights online.

The EU also called on Meta in July to change the "addictive design" of Facebook and Instagram as part of investigations under the DSA.

The world’s biggest olive oil producer is holding back 12% of its output from November to stop producer prices falling further. It’s the first time Spain has used the measure, which is expected to keep about 188,000 tonnes off the market until the end of September 2027.

Spain has ordered olive oil mills to store 12% of their production from November 2026 to regulate supply by temporarily taking some oil off the market.

The measure, published on Friday in Spain’s Official State Gazette (BOE), applies to the output each mill reports producing each month. Mills can store the oil either at their own facilities or at a third-party site.

The Directorate-General for Agricultural Production and Markets said the measure excludes output reported for October and earlier months. The oil put into storage must stay off the market until 30 September 2027, the end of the season.

The decision comes as Spain expects a strong harvest and already has high stocks. According to the resolution, opening stocks stood at 357,040 tonnes, while production is forecast to reach 1,602,596 tonnes.

The expected supply could push producer prices down further. Spanish producers were getting about €3 a kilo for extra virgin olive oil in early November, down from around €4 a kilo a year earlier, according to El País.

The government can take oil off the market when opening stocks and forecast output together are at least 20% above the average for the previous six seasons. This season’s figures met that condition. The agriculture ministry expects about 188,000 tonnes to be taken off the market.

Spain is the world’s largest olive oil producer and exporter, according to its agriculture ministry. The ministry estimates that Spain accounts for about 45% of global production and 70% of EU production, though those shares vary by harvest.

Olive oil prices rose sharply after drought and heatwaves hit harvests in recent years, then fell as production recovered.

Dcoop and Acesur agree to buy Deoleo Holding

The government’s decision coincides with a major deal in the sector that would bring three big names in olive oil together. Spanish companies Dcoop and Acesur have agreed to acquire Deoleo Holding, a subsidiary of listed olive oil group Deoleo.

Deoleo describes itself as the world’s largest branded olive oil company and owns brands including Carbonell and Hojiblanca.

The deal values all of Deoleo Holding at €520mn, including debt. The agreement covers a 91.99% stake, including Deoleo’s entire 50.99% holding.

If the remaining shareholders join the sale as expected, the buyers could acquire 100%. Acesur said the two buyers plan to take equal stakes. The deal requires regulatory approvals and a vote by listed Deoleo’s shareholders.

Deoleo shares closed 21.1% lower on Thursday after the announcement. The deal followed months of negotiations and a rival bid from Spain’s Migasa and Italy’s Coricelli.

Cardiologist Ilija Srdanović has become the international face of Serbia’s Student List, fielding calls from Macron, Costa and Plenković. But it is still unclear whether he will emerge as the leader of the future Serbian government.

Serbia’s Student List is winning recognition from EU institutions and governments, and one man has become the face of that outreach: a cardiologist and university professor who might become the country’s new leader.

Until two years ago, Ilija Srdanović was a little-known professor at the University of Novi Sad. Now he is the international face of the movement that has transformed Serbia’s political landscape, and the first number foreign leaders dial.

“I had a conversation with Ilija Srdanović, head of the Student List in Serbia,” French President Emmanuel Macron wrote on X on Monday. “I reiterated to him France’s friendship toward Serbia and our determination to continue supporting it on its European path.”

Macron is only the latest leader to reach out since the 25 October elections. In them, the Student List, a force born of a grassroots protest movement, ousted Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) after 14 years of complete dominance. It won 140 of the 250 seats, enough to form a government alone.

European Council President António Costa, Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, North Macedonia’s Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos all rushed to congratulate the Student List. Almost all of them used the same number: Srdanović’s.

The 56-year-old cardiologist emerged as a leading figure of the student protests that followed the Novi Sad railway station disaster, which killed 16 people on 1 November 2024.

Born in Novi Sad and raised in Vrbas, he has worked at the Institute for Cardiovascular Diseases of Vojvodina in Sremska Kamenica since 1997 and teaches at the University of Novi Sad’s Faculty of Medicine.

The tragedy became the catalyst for mass protests, as it came to symbolise the corruption of public institutions and the concentration of power under SNS rule. Srdanović became an outspoken critic of Vučić, notably over the police’s violent repression of the protests and interference in academic autonomy.

“Those who are not aware that this unstoppable wave is present in society today and cannot understand it, unfortunately, are not worthy of the time they are in and do not serve this historical moment,” he told the Serbian daily Nova in September 2025.

Two months ago, he was named to head the Student List’s slate of 250 candidates, making him one of Serbia’s most recognisable public figures.

On foreign policy, Srdanović has publicly affirmed the Student List’s commitment to EU membership, and to anti-corruption, judicial independence and media freedom. “We remain committed to European integration,” he told Radio Free Europe in an interview published on 27 October.

However, the Student List grew out of a heterogeneous movement, with worldviews ranging from the radical left, such as sociologist Jovo Bakić, to more conservative figures. It was united not by a shared ideology but by a demand for change and opposition to SNS rule.

Its campaign was fought purely on domestic ground, with little attention paid to Serbia’s international orientation. So while Srdanović has already announced that better relations with neighbours will be a priority, there are points on which Serbia’s foreign policy is unlikely to change.

The most significant one for Brussels might be the lack of alignment with the EU on sanctions against Russia, as many Serbs still remember how Western sanctions against Slobodan Milošević’s regime hurt the population.

On Kosovo, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama told Euronews that the Student List was unwilling to discuss recognition, and that “the music in Belgrade will not change”. Srdanović has said dialogue with Pristina should continue, but has left open a review of agreements reached so far.

Srdanović is not the only prominent figure in the Student List, which has yet to agree on its leadership structure and the composition of the government. The movement’s elected lawmakers will vote on it.

Euronews can confirm that he was not part of the four-person delegation that met Commissioner Kos in Brussels on Monday, the first high-level meeting between the Student List and the EU executive. The meeting was not announced in advance, and the European Commission declined to name the attendees.

That reticence reflects the fact that the delegation’s members are not yet MPs and the old Vučić-led establishment formally remains in power. The group aims to agree on guidelines covering energy use, infrastructure, water resources, community involvement, economic benefits, transparency and accountability, as well as how the measures should be put into practice.

With technology companies and environmental groups taking part, the document sets out rules for the discussions, encouraging members to "check your assumptions by asking clarifying questions" and "attack problems, not people."

The meetings will also follow the "Chatham House rules" which means "conversations stay in the room and learnings leave (without attribution)."

New power plants have driven up electricity bills, while data centres also generate noise pollution. Their cooling systems can use large amounts of municipal water, and mist from cooling towers can carry harmful bacteria.

To avoid increasing electricity costs for local residents, some newer data centres generate their own power, often using noisy, polluting gas-fired plants.

In the US, growing concerns over the environmental impact of data centres and rising electricity costs have sparked protests in several communities.

The European Union and the United Kingdom are preparing to reconnect their carbon markets, a move that could spare manufacturers on both sides of the Channel from additional carbon border charges, according to a draft document seen by Euronews.

The two sides are expected to announce the conclusion of negotiations to link their respective Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), allowing EU and British carbon allowances to be mutually recognised.

The move would address a growing trade concern following the introduction of the EU's carbon border mechanism in January 2026 and Britain's plans to introduce its own system in January 2027.

Without a formal link between the two carbon markets, manufacturers could face additional carbon costs when exporting goods across the Channel, despite already operating under domestic emissions pricing systems.

Protecting industrial competitiveness?

Some EU and UK officials have argued that energy-intensive industries such as steel, aluminum, cement and fertilisers could avoid additional charges, which could help protect competitiveness and reduce the administrative burden of trading between the two markets.

But the proposed linkage has its critics.

British MP David Tufnell said the country's industry is at a "critical juncture," blaming high carbon costs for the industrial decline.

"Pursuing UK-EU ETS linkage threatens to push UK carbon prices up even further towards EU levels," Tufnell told Euronews.

Carbon markets are designed to encourage industries to invest in decarbonisation by putting a price on emissions. But the global energy crisis and high inflation have intensified concerns about the costs of the green transition for businesses and households.

Tufnell also argued that the UK gives its industries fewer free carbon allowances than the EU, potentially leaving British manufacturers facing higher emissions costs than their European competitors.

"This matters greatly for industrial communities like mine in Pembrokeshire and for British industrial competitiveness and national resilience more broadly. If carbon costs rise faster in the UK than in competing jurisdiction then production, investment and employment move overseas while global emissions remain unchanged,” Tufnell said.

But closer integration would also bring regulatory obligations, a politically sensitive issue in Britain, where Brexit was partly driven by the desire to escape EU rules.

The two carbon markets have different rules and sectoral coverage, including differences over the treatment of transport and buildings.

Moreover, the second EU ETS iteration, which will mandate oil and gas operators to pay for the emissions linked to heating in buildings and road transport fuels, is due to kick in in 2029. If the EU and the UK link their carbon markets, Britain would be required to keep its carbon pricing sufficiently aligned with EU requirements.

EU officials are keen to extend the reach of its carbon-pricing system beyond the bloc's borders, while protecting the integrity of its market against carbon leakage.

The UK sees it as an opportunity to reduce trade costs and preserve access to the European market without formally rejoining the EU's regulatory structures.

Ukraine has shared the names of more than half a million Russian soldiers, but fewer than 1% have been added to the EU’s Schengen security database. Brussels is now exploring ways to overcome the legal hurdles amid growing concerns over Russian security threats.

EU countries are struggling to keep Russian soldiers and war veterans out of Europe because of legal and bureaucratic obstacles that have prevented them from adding hundreds of thousands of names to the bloc's shared security database.

Ukraine has supplied European authorities with the identities of more than half a million Russian soldiers, amid growing fears that combatants returning from the frontline could pose a security threat.

But after almost a year of work, EU countries have managed to enter fewer than 1% of those names into the Schengen Information System (SIS), which border guards use to identify people who should be refused entry.

Ukraine has been compiling a database of Russian soldiers identified on the frontline and systematically sharing it with Estonia. Tallinn, in turn, passes the information to countries including Germany, Lithuania, Poland and Czechia.

In recent months, officials in these countries have been painstakingly entering the names into SIS, the EU's main shared database for security, border management and law enforcement.

Border guards routinely consult it when checking travellers at the external borders, and police can use it for law-enforcement purposes.

Originally conceived as a security measure to compensate for the abolition of internal border controls within the Schengen area, the system has gradually expanded to cover a much broader range of security and migration alerts.

There is, however, a practical and legal obstacle. SIS was not designed as a mass watchlist of foreign military personnel who have never set foot in Europe. Its legal framework requires authorities to establish specific grounds for each alert, including an individual assessment of the threat a person poses.

As a result, countries trying to keep Russian combatants out have had to work within a system built around individual alerts and decisions, not a blanket mechanism for flagging entire categories of foreign nationals.

Individual assessments

Kyiv typically shares information identifying Russian soldiers and their alleged involvement in the war, along with details such as their location on the frontline. That does not automatically meet the legal bar for an SIS entry.

Under EU rules on SIS alerts for refusal of entry and stay, national authorities must carry out an individual assessment and establish that the person’s presence would threaten public policy, public security or national security.

This means authorities cannot simply upload Ukraine’s database into SIS. They must gather and assess further information on each person, establish the legal grounds and take a formal decision before issuing an alert. The process is lengthy and resource-intensive, especially for a database of hundreds of thousands of names.

Given the high death toll among Russian troops on the frontline, some of those listed may already be dead. Despite these inefficiencies, national authorities have been left with no better option.

“At this stage, we have nothing better to do than put these people in the SIS; it’s the most effective system,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, noting that when one member state enters a name, the alert becomes binding on all the others.

It is not the first time national authorities have run into this problem. A very similar case arose with former ISIS members, but those numbered a few hundred, not hundreds of thousands.

Ban on combatants

EU institutions and governments have therefore spent recent months discussing technical ways to bar current and former Russian combatants from European soil.

The issue was a sticking point in negotiations on the latest sanctions package against Russia, adopted in July, and was watered down at the insistence of Italy and France.

Under the final compromise, the package does not apply the combatants ban directly but makes it conditional on implementing measures. The Commission is working on them and could present them as early as the next Foreign Affairs Council on 16 November.

Meanwhile, Russia’s hybrid threats have become increasingly physical. The most prominent case is the attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport in August, which Berlin formally attributed to Moscow in September.

Shifting security landscape

The episode has shifted perceptions of the Russian threat across Europe. Northern and eastern European countries are pushing to restrict tourist visas for Russians, while the likes of Italy, France and Spain issue them in large numbers.

At an informal ministerial meeting in early September, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said there was “broad support” for moving forward with a ban on tourist visas for Russian soldiers and war veterans.

“The moment you say it was Russia, you need to react, or you are inviting more attacks. France understands this and has moved; it is only Italy standing in the way now,” a second EU diplomat told Euronews on condition of anonymity.

While France’s position appears to have shifted, Italy remains sceptical, fearing its consular services would be overloaded identifying Russian ex-combatants among visa applicants, as well as potential legal challenges.

Rome, however, faces an awkward fact: one of the main suspects in the Leipzig attempted attack was a Belarusian citizen who entered the EU on a tourist visa issued by the Italian consulate in Minsk. The other was a Russian-born Latvian citizen.

Political opposition seems to be gradually giving way, but the question remains technical and, above all, legal. EU officials fear a flood of court challenges, which makes finding a solid solution all the more pressing.

Technical solutions

The EU delegation in Moscow initially held several rounds of consultations with member states' consulates on operational challenges. But consular procedures are not the main obstacle, and arrangements are expected to be put in place relatively quickly.

A Commission paper circulated during the last sanctions negotiations, seen by Euronews, proposed expanding the list of supporting documents Russians must submit for an EU visa to include military booklets for men of conscription age.

Officials also worry about circumvention: Russian authorities might systematically forge the booklets or even supply entirely false identities. That is why certain EU countries, like Czechia, only allow Russians with biometric passports to enter.

“The question is not so much whether we will respond or not but if the measure will be solid or not,” an EU official with direct knowledge of the matter told Euronews. “We need to put a system in place, but we also need to make sure it cannot be circumvented.”

A longer-term fix would be to amend the Schengen Borders Code, giving member states more flexibility in managing SIS and moving from individual listings to a new category covering people believed to pose a security threat.

This could be paired with a revision of the Visa Code, which the Commission is expected to propose in early 2027, giving the EU the power to adopt coordinated restrictions on specific categories of travellers, including combatants from an aggressor state.

Diplomatic restrictions

A separate track concerns further limits on the movement of Russian diplomatic and consular staff, also seen as a security liability amid escalating hybrid attacks.

The 19th sanctions package already restricted Russian diplomats’ movement by requiring them to notify authorities in a second member state before travelling to or transiting through it.

But while advance notification is mandatory, an optional mechanism requiring diplomats to obtain prior authorisation has largely gone unused.

Across these initiatives, the EU faces the same challenge: finding a practical, legally sound solution that preserves a coordinated European approach while delivering a firm response to Russia's hybrid threats.

Două campanii notorii asociate Rusiei au vizat alegerile din Franța.

Matryoshka, care distribuie zilnic aproximativ o duzină de materiale false, prezentate ca provenind de la instituții de presă consacrate sau de la experți, este cea mai prolifică dintre acestea, potrivit lui Chine Labbé, vicepreședintă pentru parteneriate și redactor-șef pentru Europa la NewsGuard.

„Până la jumătatea lunii octombrie 2026, număraserăm 89 de materiale false produse de Matryoshka care vizau candidații la alegerile prezidențiale din Franța.”

The 20-member cleaning team has created the largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean.

With the longest coastline of any country on the Mediterranean, Greece is blessed with sandy beaches, rocky coves and idyllic islands. But it also faces a rubbish problem – especially on inaccessible shores.

That's where the Typhoon comes in, a 72-metre-long vessel dedicated to cleaning up the Greek coastline. Every day, its 20-member cleaning crew gathers, sorts and documents between 500-1,000 kilograms of waste.

Over the past seven years, the Typhoon Project has completed over 10,000 clean up operations, retrieving 1,140 tonnes of trash – enough to fill around 22 Olympic-sized swimming pools or 1,160 large shipping containers – from remote shores that are not connected to the roads or businesses.

In most cases, it is not litter left by swimmers on the beach, but waste carried there by sea currents.

That is how a beer can with an advert in Spanish for a World Cup from the 1990s ended up on the islet, Patroklos. It lies in the Saronic Gulf, around 65 nautical miles from Athens.

The programme, which began in July 2019, is an initiative of the Public Benefit Foundation 'Athanassios C. Laskaridis'. By February 2023 the first cycle of clean-ups of the island and most of the mainland coastline had been completed.

'The largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean'

Accessing the shores on five inflatable boats, the team gathers waste and takes it on board the ship. But their work does not end there. Besides sorting and transporting the waste to be recycled in the appropriate facilities, there is also the recording and analysis of the data, which is just as important.

"One part of the project is collecting the waste, but the second is collecting the data. We carry out detailed recording of all the waste. We know exactly what quantity there is, how many kilos, how many items from each beach. At the moment we have the largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean, and we are developing it every day," Thanasis Besios, manager of the Typhoon Project, tells Euronews.

The Public Benefit Foundation 'Athanassios C. Laskaridis' started its activities around nine years ago and focuses on three main pillars: protecting the environment, and especially the sea, supporting micro-entrepreneurship and making donations to third parties for the common good.

After seven years of activity in Greek waters, the Typhoon Project's tally is as impressive as it is discouraging.

"With the Typhoon we have collected more than 1,140 tonnes of waste. To help people picture it in their minds, we are talking about 22 Olympic-size swimming pools or around 1160 large containers," notes Peggy Xirotagarou, Executive Director at the Public Benefit Foundation 'Athanassios C. Laskaridis'.

'A large proportion of the waste comes from inland'

But pollution is not a problem that affects only the sea. In many places across the country, uncontrolled, illegal landfills are still operating.

"By observing the waste we were finding on the shores, we realised that a large proportion came from inland. So, in 2024, we created a new programme, called Cyclone. It involves large-scale clean-ups in lakes, rivers and archaeological sites. We have created three large teams in different parts of Greece, where every day we collect more than 1,000 kilos of waste," says Peggy Xirotagarou.

The Typhoon Project cooperates with the Laboratory of Marine Geology and Physical Oceanography of the Department of Geology at the University of Patras to study benthic waste in the Saronic and Thermaic Gulfs, and with the Marine Remote Sensing Research Group of the University of the Aegean to locate and map plastics using modern technology.

It also organises activities with the schools on the islands it visits.

"In every place we visit, we have a holistic approach. Our work is not limited to clean-ups. There are educational programmes that we have designed and run. So in every place we go we also bring the schools in. We go into the classrooms and take the children to the beaches to raise their awareness. Because that is the ultimate goal. For them to become responsible citizens and for this reckless use of single-use plastics to stop," Peggy Xirotagarou tells Euronews.

Essentially a companion piece to McDonagh's debut 'In Bruges', 'Wild Horse Nine' can feel like familiar ground. However, John Malkovich makes every acerbic, funny and at times surprisingly moving line of dialogue a joy to watch, and he's a shoo-in for Best Actor at next year's Oscars.

At this point, it wouldn't be a Martin McDonagh joint without two lonely and dysfunctional souls seeking a warped connection in a world that seems hellbent on imperilling the possibility of redemption.

For his latest black comedy, Wild Horse Nine, the British-Irish writer-director harks back to his feature debut In Bruges - except it's out with two bickering hitmen in Belgium and in with a squabbling pair of CIA operatives on Easter Island prior to the 1973 Chilean coup.

Taking a break from disrupting democracy, seasoned and increasingly forgetful agent Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell), who doesn't mind killing a man while eating a burger, are on holiday. Sort of. The odd couple plan to take in the sights of Rapa Nui, visit the giant stone heads – sorry, Moai - and verbally piss off two pro-Salvador Allende students (Mariana di Girolamo, Ailín Salas) who they keep bumping into.

But everything is not as it seems. Despite his Memento-style notes, Chris' cognitive decline has led him to forget that the trip is also his last hurrah. Not only does he have a bad case of oversharing and wrestles with existential malaise regarding the regimes he's toppled (with a side helping of Catholic guilt), he also riddled with cancer. With not long left, Chris previously asked Lee to Of Mice And Men him on the trip.

He's forgotten that detail, but not his wish to work on his memoir, which he dictates into a tape recorder. These tapes are a source of great discomfort for the pair's boss, chief spook MJ (Steve Buscemi), who fears Chris' indiscretions and confessions - especially "the Dallas parts" which could reveal Chris' role in JFK's assassination - may jeopardise the agency...

While not deviating from his established playbook, Wild Horse Nine feels like a satisfying Best Of compilation from McDonagh, as he merges the narrative framework of In Bruges with Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri 's adoration for the F-bomb, a cheeky Tom Waits cameo (à la Seven Psychopaths), and the more quietly moving qualities at the heart of The Banshees of Inisherin. If that all sounds like your bag, there's a great time to be had.

When the balancing act works, the filmmaker's signature acerbic wit and beloved themes surrounding salvation and unavoidability of death coalesce into a bittersweet whole. When it faulters, his script can feel like a self-indulgent succession of showboating monologues and non-sequitur-filled tangents – a niggle which has resulted in past accusations of narrative bittiness and smugness of tone.

For the most part though, McDonagh pulls it off and plays to his strengths – loading the crackling tirades with some depth. For instance, a breakfast speech explaining why "gay countries" produce better cheeses than the US illicits laughter but also directly feeds into an initially promising commentary on the historic ills of American interventionism - and ongoing horrors of US foreign policy.

Frustratingly, more could have been accomplished here considering the politically charged backdrop, and the female characters do stand out for being underused. It's a pity, as Mariana di Girolamo shines as Monica in the little screentime she is given. She is essentially relegated to being the wide-eyed embodiment of Chris' long-lost optimism, and had she been given more to do, character dynamics could have been amplified and McDonagh could have bolstered his teased critical strands. While the last act hints at transformation before a tough battle ahead, a trick was missed.

Ultimately, enjoyment rests on the double-act chemistry between the leads, which is there in spades and largely rests on Malkovich's capable shoulders. After years of forgettable bit-part roles, the veteran actor is firing on all cylinders and delivers his best performance since Being John Malkovich. Or maybe since his villainous turn as Pascal Sauvage in Johnny English, which is a performance for the ages, and we won’t hear another word about it.

Whether he’s admitting to caring more about the Chilean moths than the people of Chile, irascibly lashing out at whoever happens to be in his vicinity, or musing on why there aren’t more songs about suicidal birds, Malkovich savours every line of dialogue. His trademark elocution suits McDonagh’s prose to a T – especially when he's repeatedly enunciating the word “cahoots”.

What a wonderful word... Did you know it was originally derived from the French 'cahute', meaning a small shack, evoking the image of huddled schemers. Who's to say whether that's gospel, but as Tom Waits once said, "Most people don't care if you're telling them the truth or if you're telling them a lie, as long as they're entertained by it".

Oh god, it's gone all McDonagh with a wordy digression. Back to John...

The way Malkovich manages to simultaneously dip his toes into eccentric, amoral, melancholic and soulful terrains creates pessimistic poetry that his hard to resist. The actor already bagged the Volpi Cup for Best Actor in Venice, where the film premiered this year, and on the strength of this performance he's a shoo-in for Oscar glory next year.

Not hurting those odds is the fact that his last Oscar nomination was in 1993 for In The Line Of Fire – in which he played the unnamed killer attempting to assassinate the President of the United States. The Academy loves a comeback story; and who doesn't love a decent bit of movie-echoing symmetry masquerading as coincidence?

So, familiar ground though Wild Horse Nine may be, there's every chance you'll be hearing a lot more about this sardonic and occasionally moving yarn come awards season.

As Türkiye prepares to host the UN climate summit, one critic describes the country's climate targets and policies as “critically insufficient”.

Row after row of solar panels stretches across a vast landscape in the central Turkish province of Konya, turning sunlight into electricity – and helping Türkiye, the host of the upcoming UN climate summit, spotlight its efforts to expand renewable energy.

Still, advocates for robust action on climate change say Türkiye's cleaner energy ambitions stand in sharp contrast to its continued reliance on coal.

Campaigners also argue the country lacks concrete plans to transition away from fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal, which when burned release greenhouse gases that heat the planet.

Türkiye’s Energy Ministry says coal remained the country’s largest source of electricity last year, accounting for 33 per cent of generation. But it stressed that the share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23 per cent.

Türkiye has one of Europe's largest solar farms

The town of Karapinar in Konya is home to the Kalyon Karapınar YEKA-1 Solar Power Plant, which boasts more than three million solar panels perched on a terrain equivalent to the size of 2,600 football fields.

Operational since 2023, it generates enough electricity each year to meet about 0.7 per cent of the country’s power demand, according to plant director Burak Dogru.

“We prevent approximately 1.75 million metric tons of carbon emissions every year,” Dogru told The Associated Press – evidence, he says, of how Türkiye has been directing its economy and energy sector toward cleaner energy sources.

Türkiye’s total greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, the last year for which data is available, reached 584.5 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.

Duygu Kutluay, a campaigner with the Beyond Fossil Fuels advocacy group, said Türkiye has made plans for a major push in renewable energy.

“But these plans contain neither a roadmap for a coal phase-out, nor any planning for a phase-out of other fossil fuels, including gas,” Kutluay cautioned, adding that this is "not compatible” with Türkiye's pledge to reach net-zero emissions by 2053.

Türkiye is also looking to nuclear power to reduce its energy dependence. The country’s first plant is under construction on the Mediterranean coast, with plans for additional reactors still under consideration.

Concerns and criticism rise ahead of the COP31 summit

Some 265 kilometres away from Konya, the 9-20 November summit in the Mediterranean city of Antalya will bring together tens of thousands of delegates, world leaders, business and civil society representatives for discussions on implementing climate goals.

The summit – officially, the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 – comes against a backdrop of deepening concerns over energy security and the Iran war, which has led to a rise in gas and oil prices and sent countries scrambling to meet energy needs.

Many experts have recently argued that a key mission – combating climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions – has been failing.

The United States, the world’s richest nation and second-biggest carbon polluter after China, will again be absent from the summit, after US President Donald Trump withdrew the US from global climate negotiations.

And the last two summits have ended with little agreement on how to reduce emissions, the final texts not even mentioning fossil fuels.

Türkiye’s environment and climate change minister, Murat Kurum, who will preside over the summit, has said he wants COP31 to focus on turning climate commitments into action rather than new targets.

To that aim, Türkiye will push a “climate implementation bridge”, an initiative to help countries turn climate pledges into action by connecting them with financing, technology and other support.

“Today, the world is not merely waiting for new decisions," Kurum said while presenting summit priorities earlier this year. "What the world wants is to see past decisions put into practice.”

Türkiye has cast itself as an environment steward

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has insisted his country is committed to environmental protection and combating climate change, and first lady Emine Erdogan has championed a “zero waste” campaign to encourage recycling and a more responsible use of resources.

COP31 will also prioritise electrification and reduction of waste and methane emissions, Kurum has said.

However, the Climate Action Tracker, which measures countries’ progress against goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement, has described Türkiye’s climate targets and policies as “critically insufficient”.

The agreement set a target of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius compared to the early 1800s, directing countries to develop policies that would help meet that goal.

Meanwhile, human rights groups accuse Ankara of dismissing environmental concerns and frequently arresting activists.

Earlier this year, a court annulled an environmental impact assessment for a planned expansion of a coal-fired power plant at Afsin-Elbistan in southeastern Türkiye. The ruling was hailed by environmentalists as a major victory.

But shortly afterward, plans emerged to expand another coal-fired power plant in Canakkale, in the country's northwest.

Like other Mediterranean nations, Türkiye faces mounting risks from heatwaves, drought, water scarcity, wildfires and flooding. Last month, rains described as the heaviest in more than 80 years caused severe floods in Istanbul, Türkiye’s largest city, and left eight people dead.

Türkiye was announced as the host of COP31 following a tug-of-war with Australia, which also wanted to host the summit. As a compromise, Australia has been leading consultations to help set the summit's agenda and will be in charge of summit discussions.

Climate advocates have slammed the summit for being awarded to coal-reliant Türkiye; coal-exporter Australia has also come under criticism.

But UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell defended the choice, saying in February that a COP host country’s status on fossil fuels does not determine the success or failure of a summit.

With “Türkiye and Australia leading this process, there is every opportunity to deliver a very strong outcome," he said.

The Indian state is encouraging visitors to discover ayurveda on their next visit, and to also come for Onam, a traditional harvest festival in September.

The Kettuvallam, a traditional houseboat, has long been a symbol of tourism in Kerala, with many visitors coming to the Indian state primarily to explore the backwaters.

But that’s certainly not the only reason to visit, with the destination offering up ayurvedic-led wellness, home stays with locals, and cultural festivals.

“Kerala is a destination for all. If your family came to Kerala and each came with different interests, we can offer something for all of them,” P.C. Vishnunadh, Minister for Tourism and Culture for the Government of Kerala, told Euronews Travel at World Travel Market in London.

“You might be coming to see the backwaters, but you can also experience the forest, the beach, our culture, our culinary offering, everything is here.”

The home of ayurveda

Kerala’s tourism board is encouraging visitors to experience its ayurveda offering in 2027 and beyond.

If you’re not familiar with ayurveda, the alternative medicine system goes far beyond just massages, with special diets, meditation and other therapies, and is something that has been practiced in India for thousands of years.

“If you are coming to an ayurvedic resort, the doctors will assess your physical situation and come up with a complete treatment plan,” Vishnunadh added.

“It’s wellness, but it’s not just massage, we can offer treatments based on thousands of years of knowledge.”

Wellness retreats have become hugely popular in recent years, and travellers are increasingly looking for new and interesting experiences in that realm.

Tourism that benefits locals

Another big trend in travel is looking at how tourism can benefit local communities.

Kerala is leaning into this by working together with locals who want to offer home stays, giving them subsidies and other forms of assistance such as training.

“Hotels and resorts are owned by big corporations, whereas home stays are operated by our local people,” Vishnunadh noted.

“Local village people who are offering one or two rooms within their house will benefit from steady employment, but they are also becoming part of our tourism network.”

While it’s not ready yet, the tourism board plans to launch a directory of these home stays to make it easier for tourists to book a room.

Introducing Onam to the world

Kerala Tourism is also looking to promote Onam, a traditional harvest festival, to foreign tourists for the first time.

Taking place over the course of 10 days, the dates of Onam are based on the Malayalam calendar. The festival begins during the month of Chingam, which typically falls between August and September. In 2027, it will begin on 12 September.

The festival is a riot of colours, and begins with the Athachamayam parade where elephants march alongside floats that depict scenes from historical and mythological tales.

You’ll also see dancers painted to look like tigers completing traditional dances, and the season is also associated with snake boat races that see hundreds of people compete on the Pampa River.

For foodies, you won’t want to miss the Onam sadya, or feast. Unsurprisingly for a harvest festival, the feast features plenty of seasonal vegetables.

Served on plantain leaves, there are traditionally nine courses featuring curries, soups, dal and traditional desserts.
